opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, it was humbling. I came into MIT feeling fairly confident because I'd done a lot of competition-style math, olympiad problems where you find the clever trick and the whole thing unravels. Graduate probability was a very different kind of math. It wasn't about one beautiful insight. It was measure theory underneath everything, sigma-algebras, convergence theorems, and you had to be extremely careful about what you were allowed to say. My intuition kept running ahead of what I could actually prove.

At first I took it personally. I thought, maybe I'm not as good at this as I believed. But over time I realized the difficulty was telling me something useful. Being fast and being deep are two different skills. Competition math rewards speed and pattern-matching. Research-level math rewards patience, building a framework, and sitting in confusion for a long time without panicking.

So I changed how I worked. I stopped trying to solve problem sets in one sitting. I'd rewrite proofs from the textbook in my own words, ask why each hypothesis was there, and try to break the theorem by removing one. I spent a lot of time in office hours and with classmates who were further along, and I learned not to be embarrassed asking basic questions.

Looking back, it was one of the most important experiences I had there. It taught me rigor isn't pedantry. It's what lets you trust your own reasoning. That idea has stayed with me, and it's part of why I care so much now about formal verification and making mathematical reasoning something you can check, not just something that feels right.

r001.rationale: The response says graduate probability was challenging because it required measure-theoretic rigor and patience, but it does not attribute the difficulty to a weak foundation in analysis.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the honest answer is that it took me a while to make sense of it at all. I'd done well in math competitions, I'd done well in undergraduate courses, and then I walked into that graduate probability class and for the first few weeks I genuinely could not follow what was happening on the board. The measure-theoretic foundations, the way the professor would compress three steps into one line, the sheer pace of it. I remember sitting there thinking, everyone else seems fine, so the problem must be me.

What helped was realizing that "the problem is me" was both true and not very useful. Yes, there were gaps in my background. But the gaps weren't a verdict on whether I belonged there. They were just a list of things to go learn. So I went back to the foundations I'd skipped over, I started working problems from scratch rather than reading solutions, and I made myself go to office hours even when I felt embarrassed about how basic my questions were.

The other thing I learned, and this was more of a mindset shift, is that difficulty in mathematics is not a signal that you've reached your limit. It's the default state. If a course feels easy, you're probably not learning anything new. The discomfort of not understanding is what it feels like right before you understand something. That reframing changed how I approached everything afterward, including the research I'm doing now. When I hit a wall, I try to treat it as information about where the real problem lives, rather than as evidence about whether I'm capable of solving it.

And honestly, in hindsight, I'm grateful for that course. It was the first time I'd failed at something I cared about in a way that couldn't be fixed by just working harder in the same direction. I had to work differently. That's a lesson you can only learn by struggling.

r001.rationale: The candidate mentions gaps in her background and skipped measure-theoretic foundations, but does not clearly identify a weak foundation in analysis as the cause.

astra-6.text: I think the difficult part was separating “I’m struggling with this course” from “I’m not good at mathematics.” Those can feel like the same statement when you’re in the middle of it, but they’re very different. I tried to think about what, specifically, I wasn’t understanding, rather than treating the whole experience as a verdict on my ability. You can take the difficulty seriously without making it your identity.

r001.rationale: The response describes separating course difficulty from a judgment about mathematical ability, but does not attribute the difficulty to a weak foundation in analysis.

sol-6.1.text: I think the important distinction was between finding the course difficult and deciding that the difficulty meant I wasn’t capable. Those are very different things. A hard course can reveal gaps in your preparation or push you toward a way of thinking you haven’t developed yet. It doesn’t have to be a verdict on whether you belong in mathematics.
